title: Reverse Linked List
summary: Reverse a singly linked list in place. Walk the list with three pointers: save `next`, point `curr.next` back at `prev`, then step both forward. When `curr` falls off the end, `prev` is the new head.

complexity.note: Each node's pointer is flipped once.

intuition: Everything before `curr` is already reversed and starts at `prev`.
Save `curr.next` before overwriting it, or the rest of the list is lost.
The loop ends with `curr == null`; return `prev`.
The recursive version is elegant but uses O(n) stack.
pitfalls: Overwriting `curr.next` before saving it.
Returning `head` (now the tail) instead of `prev`.
Forgetting that the old head's `next` must become null.

Python.code:
def reverseList(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
    return prev

title: Linked List Cycle
category: Linked List · Fast and slow pointers
summary: Detect whether a list loops back on itself, in O(1) space. Move `slow` one step and `fast` two steps. If there's a cycle, fast laps slow and they meet; otherwise fast reaches null.

complexity.note: Once both are in the cycle, the gap closes by one each step.

intuition: In a cycle, the faster runner must eventually catch the slower one.
Each step, the distance between them shrinks by exactly one, so fast can't jump over slow.
Check `fast != null && fast.next != null` before moving fast.
pitfalls: A HashSet of visited nodes works but uses O(n) space.
Checking `slow == fast` before the first move (they start equal).
Forgetting `fast.next != null` and crashing on even-length lists.

def reorderList(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> None:
    if not head or not head.next:
        return
    slow = fast = head
    while fast.next and fast.next.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    second, prev = slow.next, None
    slow.next = None
    while second:
        nxt = second.next
        second.next = prev
        prev = second
        second = nxt
    first, second = head, prev
    while second:
        n1, n2 = first.next, second.next
        first.next = second
        second.next = n1
        first, second = n1, n2

title: LRU Cache
category: Linked List · Hash map + doubly linked list
summary: A cache with O(1) get and put that evicts the least recently used key when full. A hash map finds nodes by key; a doubly linked list keeps them in usage order, most recent at the front. Every access moves the node to the front; eviction removes the node before the tail.

complexity.note: Map lookups and list relinking are both O(1).

intuition: Map: key → node, for O(1) lookup.
Doubly linked list: O(1) removal from the middle and insertion at the front.
Dummy head and tail nodes remove all null checks.
On put, if the key is new and the cache is full, evict `tail.prev`.
pitfalls: Forgetting to update recency on get.
Evicting before checking whether the key already exists.
Not removing the evicted key from the map.

title: Merge k Sorted Lists
summary: Merge k sorted lists into one. Put the head of every list in a min-heap keyed by value. Repeatedly pop the smallest node, attach it to the result, and push its successor.

complexity.note: N total nodes; the heap never holds more than k nodes.

intuition: The next node of the answer is always one of the k current heads.
A min-heap returns the smallest head in O(log k).
After taking a node, its `next` becomes that list's new head.
pitfalls: Pushing null heads into the heap throws an exception.
Merging lists one by one is O(N·k).
Divide and conquer (pairwise merging) is the other O(N log k) solution.
